subject: Business
title: Measuring Product-Market Fit
description: A quick win: understand Measuring Product-Market Fit.

hook.text: Your users are growing, but does that mean you have product-market fit? Not necessarily.

buildup.text: Sean Ellis proposed a benchmark: survey users and ask how they'd feel without your product.

discovery.text: If 40% or more say 'very disappointed,' you likely have fit. Below that, keep iterating.

twist.text: Growth can mask a lack of fit. Paid ads drive signups, but retention tells the real story.

climax.text: Track cohort retention over 8 weeks. If the curve flattens above zero, your product has staying power.

punchline.text: Growth without retention is a leaking bucket.

quiz.question: Which metric best indicates true product-market fit?

details.summary: Measuring product-market fit uses quantitative signals to confirm that a product genuinely satisfies market demand. Sean Ellis's survey asking users how they would feel if the product disappeared, retention cohorts, and organic referral rates provide concrete evidence beyond anecdotal enthusiasm.
details.whyItMatters: Entrepreneurs often prematurely claim product-market fit based on early adopter excitement. Objective metrics distinguish between niche enthusiasm and genuine mainstream demand, preventing premature scaling that burns capital on an unvalidated
takeaways: Sean Ellis's survey measures fit: 40 percent of users must say very disappointed without the product
Strong retention curves that flatten rather than dropping to zero signal real fit
Organic word-of-mouth growth without paid marketing is the strongest fit indicator

faq.question: What is the Sean Ellis test for product-market fit?
faq.answer: Ask users how they would feel if they could no longer use the product, with options: very disappointed, somewhat disappointed, not disappointed. If over 40 percent choose very disappointed, you likely have product-market fit. Below 40 percent, the product needs improvement before scaling.

faq.question: Can a company have product-market fit in one segment but not others?
faq.answer: Absolutely. A product might be essential for small business owners but irrelevant to enterprises. Measuring fit by segment prevents misleading aggregate numbers. A 30 percent overall score might mask a 60 percent score among your true target segment and near zero elsewhere.
